sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Nîmes sets on-street charges by zone and has recently changed both the rules and the politics. From 2 October 2023 the tariff in the city-centre red zone was 1 euro for 40 minutes and 1.50 euros for an hour, and in the green zone 1 euro for an hour and 4.50 euros for seven hours, with the first 30 minutes free once a day per vehicle and a flat 25-euro post-parking charge [0]. The on-street concession run by the public company SPL Agate grew to 4,829 contracted spaces on 2 October 2023, with 283 pay machines, while takings per space fell from 2.03 euros a day in 2019 to 1.76 euros in 2023 [1]. Inspectors made 458,931 checks in 2023 and issued 51,215 post-parking charges, and plate-reading control was due to start in 2024 [2]. A press article of 21 December 2024 set out rules due from 1 January 2025: payment Monday to Friday 9:00 to 12:00 and 14:00 to 19:00 and Saturday mornings, an 8-hour maximum, and the flat 25-euro charge [3].

The low-emission zone was due from 1 January 2025 for the whole commune, restricting only unclassified vehicles at first, according to a city press release of 28 October 2024; we did not find its current status [4]. Around the Arènes, the city planned in February 2024 to close five streets at Porte de France to traffic, expecting the large Arènes car park to absorb displaced parking [5]. The new mayor, Vincent Bouget, suspended a planned 318-space car park near the congress centre on 14 April 2026 after resident opposition [8]; developers Tissot and GGL had presented a revised city-centre project with 318 spaces in February 2026, and the permit was still under review [9].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The new developments are mostly plans. Besides the suspended Placette car park and the Tissot and GGL project [8][9], the Nîmes Métropole president asked the State in April 2026 for 80,000 euros towards a 100,000-euro preparation phase for a multimodal hub at Caveirac, linked to the planned T5 bus line [6]. The T2 high-service bus line was reported in 2022 to include a 400-space park-and-ride at Paloma [7]. Indigo opened a 16-space secure bike park at the Porte Auguste car park in early 2025, replacing three car spaces, for 4 euros a month [10]. Q-Park reports installing 10 EV charge points at Jean Jaurès in 2023 as part of 82,000 euros of investment [16].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Car parks are run by Indigo, Q-Park and Interparking and on-street parking by SPL Agate, under concessions of roughly 11 to 61 years; Indigo's Arènes car park was conceded in 1968 for 61 years and Interparking holds Les Halles until 2029 [11]. Q-Park runs Jean Jaurès (466 spaces) and 1,232 on-street spaces under a 2006 contract with a 45-year term; the car park had 62,832 hourly entries in 2023, 4% fewer than in 2022 [15]. The Maison Carrée car park (545 spaces) is under a concession to 2036, with 268,859 hourly visits in 2021 against 333,466 in 2019 [14]. Operators paid the city 648,550 euros in fees in 2024, up 25%, and Arènes and Maison Carrée earned 3.3 and 2.4 million euros; Gare-Feuchères revenue was 15% below 2019 [12]. The city's own 2024 report puts average weekday occupancy at 68%, with about 800 free spaces even at peak, and says 26% of tickets are free [13].

Our data cover seven car parks with 4,168 spaces from the city's live feed, measured since 5 October 2026. Occupancy averaged about 52% on weekdays and 47% at weekends, weighted by spaces. The busiest by far is the CHU Carremeau hospital car park (891 spaces), which averaged 81% and reached full in a single reading on a Tuesday; the next are Porte Auguste (376) and Jardin de la Fontaine (217) at 61%. Arènes (879) averaged 43% and Maison Carrée (537) 32%, so the two car parks that earn most are not the fullest; Gare-Feuchères (800) averaged 48% on weekdays and 27% at weekends, a commuter pattern consistent with the city's remark about its weak revenue [12]. These are about two and a half weeks of data.
